Industry News: Latest Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K just got a firmware update

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (295 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has released a firmware patch for the upcoming Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K, according to AppleDB.
  • Last week the new Apple TV 4K officially launched, and with it an updated Siri Remote that adds a built-in speaker and Precision Finding so it’s harder to lose.
  • Although it’s rare for the Siri Remote to get firmware updates, Apple pushed out new firmware for the latest Siri Remote just yesterday per AppleDB.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has released a firmware patch for the upcoming Siri Remote for Apple TV 4K, according to AppleDB. Here’s what you should know.

Last week the new Apple TV 4K officially launched, and with it an updated Siri Remote that adds a built-in speaker and Precision Finding so it’s harder to lose.

Although it’s rare for the Siri Remote to get firmware updates, Apple pushed out new firmware for the latest Siri Remote just yesterday per AppleDB.

In a recent development, you can’t manually update your Siri Remote’s firmware. But as long as it’s sufficiently charged and connected to your Apple TV, the update will install automatically in the background.

This update is only available for the latest Siri Remote (4th gen).

If you’re interested in the new Siri Remote, but don’t want to buy a whole new Apple TV 4K, it’s available here as a $59 purchase and works with all Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD models.

I haven’t personally encountered any challenges with the latest Siri Remote since getting it last Friday, but apparently Apple discovered a problem that needed fixing.

Have you had any issued with the new Siri Remote? Let us know in the comments.

In a recent development, FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:.

How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5429 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.
  • Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S.
  • Industry observers note that in the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

Industry observers note that in the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Industry observers note that within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with Newly introduced York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

In a recent development, caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” indicates Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

According to recent reports, at Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The tech giant says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Industry observers note that among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

Industry observers note that to that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta indicates its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

Sources indicate that “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The manufacturer is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, Fresh York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other major reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company presently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

Sources indicate that that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In a recent development, in Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the manufacturer’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

Industry observers note that “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” indicates Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them major. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Sources indicate that beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the organization is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the firm’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

Sources indicate that the charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one notable difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

It has been revealed that then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

Recent findings suggest that if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is at the moment 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

In a recent development, xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also vital to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. GTA 6’s 30 FPS lock broke my PC gamer brain — until I turned on the one TV setting I swore I’d never touch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever bought a new TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.
  • For movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder.
  • And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever bought a new TV and invited a tech nerd like me into your living room, you already know I’m grabbing your remote, diving into the picture settings, and disabling motion smoothing.

For movies and prestige TV, it is a crime against humanity — turning a cinematic masterpiece into an episode of "Days of Our Lives" shot on a camcorder. I hate it. Tom Cruise hates it. You should hate it too.

And yet, here I am, playing Grand Theft Auto VI with motion smoothing cranked on, and refusing to turn it off.

In a recent development, to understand how I ended up committing TV heresy, you have to understand the shock to the system that is GTA 6’s frame rate. Coming straight from my monster PC rig playing games like Resident Evil Requiem at up to 214 FPS, dropping back down to a strict 30 FPS console lock feels like wading through treacle.

But on top of that, as I’ve seen (and you’ve seen on Digital Foundry’s test), that 30 FPS lock isn’t an actual lock. It can dip into the mid-20s during heavy scenes. Coming from super fluidity, that 30 FPS is brutal to adapt to.

So out of sheer desperation (and because we’re stuck waiting for the PC port), I broke the golden rule and toggled my TV’s smooth motion setting on.

And I hate to admit it, but it’s basically bootleg DLSS Frame Generation for your living room.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Just like PC frame generation tricks of old, your TV’s motion interpolation processor looks at two real frames from your console, guesses what should happen in between them, and inserts an artificial frame to smooth out the motion.

Industry observers note that the moment I flipped it on in GTA 6, that nauseating camera stutter when cruising down Ocean Beach vanished. Panning around a crowded street or taking a high-speed corner suddenly felt dramatically more fluid — nowhere near 60 fps, and definitely not my desktop rig, but miles smoother than the choppy presentation.

Before the AV forums come for my head with pitchforks, let’s be completely honest about the trade-offs. There is no such thing as a free lunch in frame interpolation:.

It has been revealed that because your TV has to wait for the next frame before it can invent the one in the middle, motion smooth adds latency between pressing a button and seeing the result on screen. In twitchy, competitive games, that’s a death sentence.

But in a Rockstar open-world game — where character movement is already famously weighty and deliberate — I never noticed that extra latency.

Your TV’s processor is just guessing after all, and while it is a good guesser, there are some moments of weird shimmering around fast-moving objects and some boiling around on-screen elements like subtitles. Probably compounded by the fact GTA 6 is already running its own resolution scaling tech under the hood.

Recent findings suggest that standard Game Mode and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) automatically lock out motion smoothing on many TVs. Depending on your set, you either have to turn on the dedicated low-latency Game Motion Plus mode (found on newer Samsung and LG sets) or sacrifice VRR to unlock it.

The silver lining, though, is that with this being a 30 FPS game, it’s not high enough to require VRR anyway.

If GTA 6’s 30 FPS cap is giving your eyes a workout and you want to test the dark arts yourself, don’t just blindly max out every slider.

If your TV has a low-latency interpolation option (like Samsung’s Game Motion Plus or LG’s TruMotion tweaks), use that before turning off Game Mode completely.

Set Judder Reduction to a middle ground (around 5-7 out of 10) rather than maxing it out. You want to take the harsh edge off camera pans without turning your car into a blurry smudge.

This is optional based on personal taste. Test how your TV’s smoothing looks with GTA’s built-in motion blur turned off. For a lot of OLED owners, letting the TV handle the smoothing cleanly beats stacking two different blur effects on top of each other.

In a recent development, do I want to play GTA 6 at native 240 FPS on my PC rig? Obviously. The second Rockstar drops the PC version, I’ll be uninstalling this hack from my brain and never looking back.

I still wouldn’t be caught dead watching a movie with motion smoothing turned on. But until PC gamers get their turn in Vice City, breaking the ultimate TV rule is the best survival trick I’ve found for making a 30 FPS masterpiece actually feel better to play.

According to recent reports, also yes, my wife has taken note of the fact that I share the same name as the male protagonist. And yes, she is side-eyeing how I treat Lucia hard.

#28342. Why the Airbus A321XLR often gets stuck climbing for first few hours of flight

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

Why the Airbus A321XLR often gets stuck climbing for first few hours of flight

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Airbus A321XLR is revolutionizing transatlantic travel, but there is a painful catch to its revolutionary range.
  • Industry observers note that an airplane cannot just take off and soar to its final cruising altitude on a long-range flight.
  • In a recent development, as the flight progresses, the engines consume fuel at a rate of several tons per hour, causing the aircraft's overall mass to drop steadily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Airbus A321XLR is revolutionizing transatlantic travel, but there is a painful catch to its revolutionary range. It must be trapped at low altitudes for the first few hours of a trip. Since an aircraft's most fuel-efficient altitude varies dynamically as it burns off fuel weight, the long-range narrowbody and many other long-haul aircraft spend a large percentage of their flight time actively rising.

Industry observers note that an airplane cannot just take off and soar to its final cruising altitude on a long-range flight. When an airliner first takes off, its fuselage is heavily laden with thousands of gallons of jet fuel required to cross an ocean or reach a distant continent. Step climbing is a dynamic operational technique designed to maximize fuel efficiency by matching an aircraft’s altitude to its changing weight over the course of a long-haul journey.

In a recent development, as the flight progresses, the engines consume fuel at a rate of several tons per hour, causing the aircraft's overall mass to drop steadily. Once the onboard flight computers calculate that the aircraft has shed enough weight to make a higher altitude aerodynamically advantageous, the crew requests permission from air controllers to climb. The flight crew will repeat this entire sequence multiple times during an eight-to-eleven-hour trip, burning off fuel, and stepping up to the next flight level.

The A321XLR pushes the physical limits of a narrowbody platform, necessitating a performance trade-off between total range and early-flight efficiency and speed. Airbus had to design a jet that could carry payloads in order to convert a domestic workhorse into a single-aisle transatlantic endurance aircraft. The end product is a narrowbody with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 223,000 lb (101,000 kg), far more than any A321 variant before it.

According to recent reports, the A321XLR cannot effectively climb to higher altitudes at maximum MTOW because it needs a lot of lift to stay airborne until it sheds weight. In the thin, less dense air at cruising flight levels around 37,000 feet (11,200 m), the A321XLR’s wing simply cannot generate enough lift. If the aircraft tries to force its way to these higher altitudes too early, it would have to fly at a high angle of attack. Not only would it result in significant drag and fuel waste, but it would also increase the risk of a stall.

Pilots of the A321XLR are specifically warned in official training that early cruising levels will be severely restricted when the aircraft lifts off beyond 85% MTOW, frequently topping out at just 32,000 feet (9,700 meters). Unlike the rocket-like ascent typical of an empty or smaller single-aisle jet, the last stages of reaching those early altitudes are infamously slow, with the climb rate dropping to a taxing 500 feet per minute.

According to recent reports, the huge fuel tank built right into the cargo bay of the A321XLR is responsible for its enormous range. Depending on the mission, airlines could install or delete optional auxiliary center tanks in the belly hold of earlier long-range models, such as the A321LR. Airbus abandoned this modular strategy for the XLR and completely reworked the bottom fuselage. The airplane has an enormous overall capacity of almost 10,500 gallons (39,747 liters) when the conventional wing and center tanks are added.

Behind the main landing gear compartment is the jet's conformal Rear Center Tank. By making the tank walls an integral part of the airplane's structural shell, Airbus maximized fuel volume without eating up all the underfloor baggage space. This specialized tank design allows the narrowbody to carry an extra 3,408 gallons (12,900 liters) of fuel.

While this engineering feat unlocks an 11-hour, 4,700-nautical-mile range, it creates a severe weight-and-balance headache the moment those tanks are topped off. Because the RCT is physically welded into the aft fuselage, the aircraft carries a permanent structural weight penalty even when flying empty. If an airline flies the XLR on a short 2-hour domestic hop with the rear tank empty, it must burn extra fuel just to carry the dead weight.

It has been revealed that to overcome the weight of its massive fuel load, the A321XLR must perform a calculated, multi-hour sequence with air traffic control known as step climbing. The flight crew must climb to a lower, temporary altitude, level off, and wait. Airbus flight manuals explicitly dictate this step-climbing technique for the XLR to keep the aircraft flying as close to its dynamically shifting optimum altitude as possible throughout a long-range mission.

This process is a slow-motion game dictated by the jet's fuel burn rate. The A321XLR consumes fuel rapidly early in the flight, about 5,000 lb (2,250 kg) of fuel every hour. As this weight burns off, the aircraft's total mass drops, the wings require less lift to maintain level flight, and the optimum cruising altitude rises. For every few tons of fuel burned, the pilots request a step-up in increments of 2,000 feet (600 m) on average.

On a typical ten-hour transatlantic crossing, an A321XLR crew will execute one or two of these step climbs before reaching their final, most efficient cruising altitude. Managing these steps requires constant coordination with air traffic controllers, who must find an open slot in the North Atlantic tracks.

It has been revealed that forcing a heavy A321XLR to its optimum altitude too early can trap pilots in a high-altitude aerodynamic bottleneck known as the 'coffin corner,' where the margin between flying and stalling virtually disappears. Officially called the 'q-corner,' this phenomenon occurs when an aircraft is flying at high altitudes where the air is thin.

Sources indicate that there, the wings require a higher speed to produce enough lift, and the aircraft's minimum safe speed, or stall speed, rises. At the same time, the speed of sound decreases in the cold, high-altitude air, lowering the aircraft's maximum safe speed. That is the critical Mach number, where air flowing over the wing goes supersonic and causes violent structural buffeting.

Sources indicate that for a heavily loaded narrowbody like the A321XLR climbing up in altitude, these two speeds begin to draw together, creating a dangerously narrow operational envelope. If a pilot flies too slowly, the heavy jet will experience a low-speed stall and fall out of the sky. If they fly too fast, shockwaves forming on the wings will cause high-speed buffeting and a loss of control. When the XLR takes off near its MTOW limit, trying to push past 32,000 feet (9,750 m) early in the flight shrinks this buffer down to a razor-thin margin of just a few knots. To avoid risk, training notes and standard operating procedures heavily caution crews against chasing the theoretical optimum altitude too aggressively.

This aerodynamic trap becomes much more acute when the aircraft encounters high-altitude turbulence or mountain waves. A sudden updraft or downdraft can instantaneously shift the angle of airflow over the wings, instantly pushing the aircraft outside its narrow safe-speed envelope. Thus, pilots will deliberately choose to fly 2,000 feet below the aircraft's technical capability, trading fuel efficiency for a safety buffer.

According to recent reports, operating thousands of feet below optimal cruise levels forces the A321XLR to plow through significantly denser air, increasing aerodynamic drag and hiking fuel consumption by an estimated 2.5% per hour. For airline accountants managing razor-thin margins on a 4,700-nautical-mile route, these initial hours of flight represent a concentrated period of fuel inefficiency. However, it is an unavoidable 'cost of doing business.'.

Recent findings suggest that while lingering in the thicker air of the lower flight levels levies a performance penalty on the plane, it inadvertently creates a widebody-style comfort upgrade that complements the A321XLR passenger experience. When an aircraft cannot climb to its optimal altitude, it pays for that safety buffer in fuel. However, this inefficiency unlocks a human benefit inside the cabin.

In a recent development, typical narrowbody aircraft cruising at high altitudes maintain an internal cabin pressure equivalent to being on top of an 8,000-foot (2,400 m) mountain. This thin cabin air is the primary culprit behind the deep physical exhaustion, pounding headaches, and severe dehydration associated with jet lag. As the A321XLR spends its heaviest initial cruise hours lower down, the equivalent altitude inside the fuselage is much lower, closer to 6,000 feet (1,800 m).

Airbus capitalized on this inevitable flight profile by integrating a new cabin pressure control standard in the Airspace Cabin. As the structural pressure differential between the inside and outside the plane doesn't have to be stretched to its absolute breaking point, the system can safely schedule a lower cabin altitude.

This dense, humid air matches the comfortable profile of an advanced widebody like Airbus' own A350 series. Passengers stepping off a transoceanic or intercontinental flight arrive feeling more refreshed than they would on an older Boeing 757, turning a performance compromise into a major traveler advantage that has helped shape how airlines market and deploy the jet worldwide.

  • Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.
  • Industry observers note that face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Industry observers note that face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

According to recent reports, use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to swiftly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

According to recent reports, if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most owners, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

According to recent reports, on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great newly introduced option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

Industry observers note that what should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that consumers have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a latest setting so owners can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

Recent findings suggest that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Sources indicate that it’s not exactly a “upcoming feature,” but iPhone Duo consumers will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and newly introduced keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it's official, and there's no escaping it — Black Friday is here. With it comes huge discounts on everything from Ninja appliances to Dyson vacuums to MacBooks and iPhones — and soundbars.

Upgrading your home cinema setup has never been cheaper (well, except maybe in like 2001 or something). Amazon has reduced the price of all its own-brand soundbars, including the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar for just $74, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus for $139, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Subwoofer for $229, and the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Subwoofer and Rears for $349.

It has been revealed that I've reviewed both the $74 2.0-channel soundbar and the $139 3.1-channel soundbar with built-in subwoofer, and both really surprised me, especially the $74 model. This is by far the cheapest soundbar I've ever awarded a 4.5-star rating — I would snap this one up for an instant TV speaker upgrade.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is the cheapest option on Amazon's home theater lineup, but it's the most surprising. With powerful bass and a fantastic dialogue mode, I didn't miss a thing during testing.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is extremely well-priced at its MSRP of $249, but $139 is almost incomprehensibly cheap. While the subwoofer can be a little boomy, if you mostly watch Netflix and YouTube, this won't be an problem at all.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer is an excellent level up. If you value clear and controlled bass, this would be the option for you. This model has clearer dialogue than the built-in subwoofer version.

For those who value true surround sound, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer and Rears is your best bet. This is the only model capable of true Dolby Atmos, so movie fanatics need look no further.

  • According to recent reports, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

According to recent reports, because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save major on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

According to recent reports, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

In a recent development, if you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

It has been revealed that the new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's right now pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

Sources indicate that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, right now marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

In a recent development, if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

It has been revealed that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Recent findings suggest that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Recent findings suggest that no. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

It has been revealed that earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Sources indicate that here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:.

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn.

Sources indicate that in a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

Recent findings suggest that one question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The organization shares just two examples of something advanced:.

In a recent development, suppose it gets it wrong like it does most of the time. I wonder if that still counts.

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”.

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”.

Industry observers note that it would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for owners. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

In a recent development, advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling upcoming approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies. Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, presently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

According to recent reports, the SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

Sources indicate that it comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple notes the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

In a recent development, if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. Octave confusion is matching a sound exactly one octave above or below the true pitch, which is half or double the frequency. Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable.

Latest Update: Fewer slides, more dragons

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a familiar sight that could send a typical tech manager into hours of procrastination and avoidant behavior:.
  • Sources indicate that it starts with a simple ask for a meeting or a presentation.
  • Sources indicate that and it gets worse when inevitably you need a coworker to contribute some content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a familiar sight that could send a typical tech manager into hours of procrastination and avoidant behavior:.

Sources indicate that it starts with a simple ask for a meeting or a presentation. No matter how pretty the template is, as soon as you decide you need “some slides,” you find yourself slinking down a path of obsessive pixel-pushing.

Sources indicate that and it gets worse when inevitably you need a coworker to contribute some content. One understandably tries to cram as much text as possible into their space in 6pt font, while another (maybe a designer) prefers short sentences with bold words. You now get to make these look like they belong in the same presentation.

Five hours later, you have the perfect build, with diagrams and animations to make your slides more compelling, educational, and memorable. As you gaze upon your mediocre masterpiece, you wonder whether those hours were worth it.

You still need to communicate information with clarity, but maybe the medium has to change.

It has been revealed that at Stripe, I have been accused of saying that we should ban slides. I may have remarked these words in anger after the fourth meeting of the week where my slides’ colors were slightly wrong because someone had pasted them in and had “matched styles in this presentation.” Most of the time, this may be an eyesore but doesn’t really matter; in this case, my green “on track” status badge had morphed into a dull yellow in the new theme.

I may not have meant it, but it’s an interesting provocation, especially when AI makes the alternatives much cheaper. Sometimes you have to take away the rotary phones to get people to use newly introduced technology.

So, I decided to try banning myself from creating slides for any reason, forcing myself to use AI to create interactive presentations instead.

Without much effort (and in under 30 minutes), you can create a Bauhaus-themed interactive strategy explainer….

Or a planetary system explaining what your team does….

This experiment has been surprisingly successful. Tired and busy Zoom brains might immediately check out when they see a slide deck, but a planetary system! Wow! That catches their attention long enough to get your point across, making meetings much more fun and efficient. And after the meeting, you can send them a link to explore the solar system on their own time. They may accidentally internalize your key points as they’re playing around with it. 🙂.

With traditional slide decks, collaboration feels like a burden. Someone might mess up your template, or use the wrong font. At the end of the day, despite your efforts, slides made by different people who own just one section will likely result in a jarring experience (or at best a “mid” experience).

Industry observers note that on the other hand, everyone has fun building low-stakes, vibe-coded webpages together. I can ask my agent to fix the layout instead of moving everything around myself. I found that after folks see others doing it, they do it themselves because it saves time while allowing them to be more creative.

Moving towards the extreme end of collaboration, I created a village of cross-org tech leads as an icebreaker exercise for an onsite. I was nervous about how it’d go given how many humans and their agents were contributing, but folks seemed to enjoy vibe-adding themselves to our tech lead village, and an old, non-AI innovation called git kept everyone’s contributions manageable.

And they kept adding to it as the day progressed.

Sources indicate that it started with a tech lead from Risk adding a dungeon and a dragon to represent the dragons the team slays for us. Inspired by that customization, others started to add their own. By the end of the day, there was a Live MaaS sign and the Pacifica Taco Bell representing the MaaS (Money as a Service) team. There was also a DEEP lake representing DEEP (Developer & End-user Experience Platform), filled with DEEP sea creatures.

Someone eventually added a way for tech leads to explore other teams, so we could see the inside of the Risk dungeon, the Pacifica Taco Bell, and the DEEP lake.

This was the first time I’d seen people engage with the creation of an icebreaker activity or presentation beyond the bounds of the activity itself. Like, it’s literally fun to code with your coworkers and riff off of each other’s ideas. It’s all low-stakes code, and our agents help us write it and make small tweaks. If a different metaphor or idea comes to mind, you can ~easily and ~cheaply start from scratch.

The village icebreaker got me rethinking other group activities I’d traditionally done in slides or Figma. Here’s a fun storybook holiday book exchange that I previously would have run in Figma, but is now interactive and ~infinitely customizable. If you’re at Stripe, you can just point your agent at the linked AGENTS.md and ask it to build one for your team on our internal infra.

This is basically just “how to vibe code a basic webpage with your friends,” but it’s worth writing down, as I find that folks sometimes hold themselves back from applying AI to well-understood use cases like creating compelling presentations.

It has been revealed that I am impatient, so I prefer simplicity above all else. In fact, I find that simple prompts work best for divergent work like brainstorming, naming, or picking a visual direction. To that end, there’s nothing super fancy or really even a “workflow” to tell you about here. I asked my agent to put these steps together:.

Recent findings suggest that have an idea you want to present. This is the most vital part. Maybe it’s a doc, some quick bullets, or a stream of consciousness you sloppily typed on your phone on the ferry ride into the office.

Ask your coding agent for a few ways to explain it. Maybe it’s a lifecycle, a planetary system, or something you haven’t thought of. Have it make quick mocks so you can see what works. (You can repeat this step until you’re happy with the concept.).

It has been revealed that pick a concept and play with the visual style. I’m a fan of pixel art and Bauhaus, but you can ask your agent to cook up a few directions. Repeat until you find something you like.

Build it and iterate. Ask your agent to change the content, tweak the visuals, or add interactions and animations. You can get much more creative than you could in slides without moving every little thing yourself.

Make it easy for others to contribute. Ask your agent to create an AGENTS.md explaining how the project works and how to contribute. Then your coworkers and their agents can take it from there.

Sources indicate that you can keep going forever, of course. I stop when I have something that gets the idea across. For me, this consistently takes less time than making slides, and my agent can crank away on iterations in the background.

In a recent development, if you’re just presenting, you can run it locally; you only need to deploy it if you want others to explore on their own. And if you need presenter mode with your script, just ask your agent to build it.

It has been revealed that my pithy learning from this experiment: AI can help us create conditions for creativity to emerge, even when doing pre-singularity activities like presentation creation and icebreakers. When you make something people want to engage with, it unlocks more ideas, opens more doors, and hatches more dragons than a slide deck ever could.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Recent findings suggest that not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before newly introduced models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Industry observers note that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The concern isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a latest tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

Industry observers note that if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

According to recent reports, yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Industry observers note that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.
