Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thegreenplace

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next".
  • It has been revealed that in this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task.
  • First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an notable step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis notes:.

It has been revealed that in this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly latest language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.

First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most key families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:.

Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.

Industry observers note that I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating latest Perl code on the fly, which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way".

Recent findings suggest that the designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:.

There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from real, hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.

In a recent development, applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we really want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach).

It has been revealed that clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:.

Recent findings suggest that all the functions used here are built-ins, including the ->> macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.

The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like "this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...", clojure.spec makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally (core.typed is another option for a more statically typed flavor).

Recent findings suggest that historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however. Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of OO-like features.

Recent findings suggest that that noted, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability to do true multiple dispatch and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.

It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many ways, which are interleaved.

First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.

Recent findings suggest that second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM.

Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises, futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.

Industry observers note that finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the core.async module. It provides two useful things:.

It has been revealed that finally, it's crucial to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless - Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.

Recent findings suggest that on the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side programming, among with some unique features like core.async for callback-free concurrency.

According to recent reports, this doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation, Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows, maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great! If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming languages.

10 Highlights Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer.
  • This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate.
  • Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other highlights dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It swiftly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

In a recent development, juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

According to recent reports, A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

It has been revealed that peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

#28228. Palo Alto Networks buys AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5bn in stock

Palo Alto Networks buys AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5bn in stock

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn.
  • Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers.
  • “Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Palo Alto Networks’ office in Singapore.

Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn. The startup helps companies train and run their own versions of open-weight AI models. Palo Alto unveiled the deal on Wednesday, minutes after The Wall Street Journal’s Kate Clark reported it.

Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers. Earlier this month it raised $350m at a $3.25bn valuation, the Journal reported. It also stated it had reached $100m in run-rate revenue. Its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer when the deal closes. The deal still needs regulatory clearance and should close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.

It has been revealed that open-weight models let users download and change the weights, the numbers that set how a model behaves. Palo Alto noted no large provider offers them securely today. It plans to let companies train, adapt and run them in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. Applied Compute will keep serving its own customers, and Palo Alto will sell the platform to its own base.

According to recent reports, arora told the Journal the deal means “venturing outside of cybersecurity”. On the earnings call, he said open-weight models now carry more than 60% of token traffic. A year ago it was under 5%.

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do,” Arora said on the call.

Palo Alto told analysts it expects the deal to add more than $1bn in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. It prepares to build more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity. Capital spending on that will stay under $3bn through fiscal 2030, it said.

Arora also addressed whether Applied Compute’s team will stay. Its staff have “millions of reasons” to stay for the next three to four years, he wrote on X. They will keep their offices and, for the most part, their independence.

Sources indicate that the deal came with Palo Alto’s fiscal first-quarter results. Revenue rose 39% to $3.44bn in the three months to 31 October. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66% to $9.73bn. Net income was $482m, up from $334m a year earlier.

Recent findings suggest that palo Alto raised its forecasts for the year. It now expects revenue of $14.52bn to $14.57bn. It sees adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share.

On the call, Arora linked part of that demand to the recent run of outages. He blamed them partly on IT teams rushing to patch AI-found flaws. He has argued before that AI prices must fall for the technology to take off. He has also called slowing AI down unrealistic.

If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying.
  • Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.
  • Recent findings suggest that the survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

Recent findings suggest that the survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

According to recent reports, if you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that you obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, you can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that if you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

#28222. Tech Report: UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (555 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: UK can’t keep its Apple encryption order secret, tribunal rules

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled.
  • In a recent development, the order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
  • “Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government can no longer keep its Apple encryption order secret, a tribunal has ruled. The Home Office had argued that confirming the order would damage national security. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected that claim in a judgment on Thursday.

In a recent development, the order is a technical capability notice under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. Such notices can require companies to change how their services work so the authorities can get access to data. Until now the Home Office had refused to confirm or deny it had served one on Apple.

“Anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges wrote.

Industry observers note that the judges said the government had not kept to its own secrecy policy. The Times and the Financial Times had reported that government sources confirmed the order. The tribunal found that those briefings took place, and that ministers, senior officials or special advisers authorised them.

It has been revealed that the Home Office noted leak investigations had found no source, but it gave the tribunal no details of them. The government had also let Apple brief senior US officials. The judges called that a further clear departure from its policy. They noted that the answer could be found by typing the question into Google’s chatbot.

The ruling does not make the order’s content public. The judges agreed that publishing all the material would damage national security. But that does not mean every detail must stay secret, they stated. The tribunal will decide that question later.

According to recent reports, the parties expect a full hearing in the first half of 2027. Much of it can now take place in public, the judges remarked. Apple has five grounds of challenge. The tribunal can decide the first two entirely in public. One asks whether the power can reach interception outside the UK. The other asks whether it can be used to regulate the security a manufacturer offers its customers.

Apple welcomed the decision as a step in the right direction for public access to the case, Bloomberg reported. Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director of Privacy International, called it a “major victory” for transparency. Privacy International and Liberty brought a separate challenge with two individuals. Liberty called the result a victory for transparency.

Recent findings suggest that the Home Office said the ruling was procedural. Apple has helped police and intelligence agencies for years, and the notice simply requires that it keeps the ability to do so, it said in a statement published by The Register.

“Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies,” a government spokesperson noted.

Recent findings suggest that apple filed its second claim in July, after the tribunal dismissed its first. In February 2025 it withdrew Advanced Data Protection for UK people. The feature extends end-to-end encryption to iCloud backups and more. Meta, TikTok and X also challenged UK data demands this autumn, from Ofcom, and reportedly lost.

A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.

In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree.

Recent findings suggest that fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. In a 5-million-member test, it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36–43%, saving up to 109 MB.

Let's take a look at why this change happened and how it works.

Large sorted sets that exceed the listpack threshold are backed by a skiplist paired with a hashtable (smaller sorted sets use a compact listpack representation that stores elements sequentially in contiguous memory). The hashtable gives O(1) lookups by member, while the skiplist gives O(log n) ordered lookups by rank or score. That pairing is architecturally simple, but the skiplist carries a significant memory cost. It stores exactly one element per node, scattered across memory as separate allocations connected by pointers.

In a recent development, valkey's skiplist pays for this in raw memory. Every node carries a backward pointer (8B), plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, since skiplists are probabilistic (each node has a 25% chance of gaining another level). Each level costs 8B for the pointer plus 8B for the span value, giving around 29B of pointer and span overhead per node. Add the 8B score, and the total reaches roughly 37B per node before accounting for the member string.

Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of hardware caches (L1, L2, and L3) to keep frequently accessed data close to the processor. These caches are much smaller and faster than main memory (RAM), so when the CPU cannot find the data it needs in its cache, it must fetch it from a slower level of the memory hierarchy. As a rough illustration, an L1 cache hit can take about 1 ns, while a DRAM access can take around 100 ns. A dependent memory access can leave the core waiting; actual latency and how much work can be hidden vary by system and workload 1.

In a recent development, each node in the skiplist is a separate allocation, potentially scattered wherever the heap happened to place it, so following the structure can require repeatedly fetching data from unrelated memory locations. Because each step can determine where the next step goes, these fetches are dependent, resulting in more round trips through the memory hierarchy. A 2025 study of concurrent in-memory indexes found that, on its tested workloads, traditional skiplists experienced roughly 2.4–4.8× more cache misses than a comparable B-tree, with 2–8× lower throughput 2 (testing different data structure implementations, not Valkey).

It has been revealed that A B+ tree keeps entries sorted in fixed-size nodes: leaf nodes hold the entries, or pointers to them, and inner nodes hold just enough routing data to pick which child to descend into. Packing many entries into each node addresses both problems above: far less per-member pointer overhead, and far fewer dependent fetches per lookup.

Industry observers note that fbtree, short for Feature B+ Tree, uses a 61-way fanout: each node can hold up to 61 entries or child pointers. Leaf and inner nodes are sized to fit jemalloc allocation classes without wasting space on 64-bit builds; on supported 32-bit builds, innerNode is rounded up to the 1280-byte class.

Recent findings suggest that A 512-byte leaf holds up to 61 value pointers, so 61 members share one node instead of each getting its own. Instead of storing the score and member separately, fbtree stores them together as a single packed value: the normalized 8-byte score followed by the member bytes. This keeps the data needed for comparisons together and removes another level of pointer indirection.

The skiplist's 25%-per-level rule gives it an effective branching factor of about 4, while fbtree's fanout is 61. Both structures retain O(log n) search complexity, but the B+ tree has substantially fewer levels to traverse and therefore fewer opportunities for expensive memory fetches.

Sources indicate that A modern CPU can also fetch several adjacent cache lines efficiently when the data is laid out contiguously, thanks in part to the way memory is accessed and to hardware prefetching 1. Therefore a B+ tree node that spans a few cache lines can be read efficiently as the CPU scans its contents.

On top of that structure, fbtree adds optimizations aimed at specific operations.

Industry observers note that in a B+ tree keyed by variable-length strings, such as sorted set members, picking a child means comparing the lookup against each child’s anchor, the largest member in that child, and reading those strings costs memory fetches. fbtree's inner nodes store each anchor along with a small four-byte "feature." Because the anchors often share a common prefix, fbtree stores that shared prefix separately and uses the four feature bytes to distinguish the children. The implementation can then compare those features in parallel using SIMD, often identifying the correct child before fetching the child node itself. If the features uniquely identify a child, the search can descend immediately; otherwise, they still narrow the range that needs a full binary search.

It has been revealed that range commands such as ZRANGE walk the set in order. fbtree links its leaf nodes in a doubly-linked list, so a scan can move from leaf to leaf without climbing back up the tree. The skiplist requests an item, waits to receive it, and only knows the next item to fetch when it's received the first. The B+ tree can work on up to 61 items in parallel, and while it works on those it can fetch the next leaf node with the next 61 items.

In a recent development, commands such as ZPOPMIN work at the ends of the set. fbtree caches its leftmost and rightmost leaves, so finding them is O(1), as in a skiplist, instead of O(log n). This keeps pop and append operations at parity rather than regressing.

Range deletions remove a contiguous run of members, and fbtree handles them without rebuilding the surrounding structure.

According to recent reports, the change is internal: sorted set commands and their behavior remain unchanged. The one visible difference is that OBJECT ENCODING returns btree instead of skiplist for a large sorted set. If you have monitoring, tests, or tooling that checks for the literal string skiplist, that's one place to patch. Small sorted sets under the listpack threshold are unaffected either way, since they never used the skiplist encoding to begin with.

The numbers below compare only the ordered index: skiplist versus fbtree, with the hashtable and member embedding unchanged.

Inserting 5 million 20-byte members sequentially reduced per-member memory overhead, excluding the member data itself, from 50.3B to 28.5B, a 43% reduction. The same 5 million members inserted in random order reduced per-member overhead from 50.3B to 32.0B, a 36% reduction.

The smaller reduction comes from random insertion leaving more partially filled nodes than sequential insertion.

Industry observers note that for the 5-million-member set in this test, that is roughly 109 MB saved with sequential inserts and 92 MB with random inserts. The savings are per member, not per byte stored, so the relative reduction in total memory is largest for sets with many small members and shrinks as member size grows.

The benchmarks below were measured on PR #4206’s oi/pr3-fbtree-v2 branch and were not rerun for the merged commit. They were run on a Graviton3 c7g.metal system with 64 cores, nine I/O threads, a pipeline depth of 10, and a 3-million-member sorted set. Each test was repeated five times; the reported confidence intervals were ≤2% for all commands except ZRANDMEMBER.

The same underlying design changes also improve throughput for several sorted set operations:.

In a recent development, ZADD and ZREM reposition elements in the tree, so they gain the most from fbtree's shallower structure and fewer pointer updates. Range operations see smaller gains because once the index traversal becomes cheap, producing and returning the requested elements becomes a larger part of the total cost. ZSCORE and ZRANDMEMBER barely move because they use the hashtable, not the ordered index.

The crucial takeaway: the commands didn't change, but in our tests large sorted sets carried 36–43% less per-member overhead, and ZADD and ZREM throughput rose 105% and 76%.

The goal wasn't simply to make the data structure faster in isolation: the implementation was repeatedly benchmarked against the existing skiplist through the full Valkey server, with optimizations added until fbtree matched or exceeded the skiplist across the tested sorted set commands.

Valkey 9.2 is right now in release-candidate testing. Before GA, try the 9.2 release candidate with your real workload, especially if large sorted sets or commands such as ZADD, ZREM, ZRANK, or ZCOUNT are key to you. Your testing and feedback can help surface problems before the final release, so open an concern with anything you find.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. Sources indicate that if Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. Sources indicate that alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

In a recent development, in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

#28213. ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS

ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ricapar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.
  • Industry observers note that backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer.
  • It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.

Industry observers note that backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.

It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.

I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.

From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.

Sources indicate that old, meet upcoming. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?

And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?

I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.

As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.

Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.

The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.

Sources indicate that every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.

According to recent reports, one message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.

The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.

ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB.

Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:.

▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube.

Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.

That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:.

And this is what Claude made of it:.

Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, indicates what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.

Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language.

A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy.

Sources indicate that eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these:.

According to recent reports, A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one.

Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories:.

According to recent reports, safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off.

Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too.

Industry observers note that any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works.

Industry observers note that easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is latest, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on.

According to recent reports, A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads.

docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back.

Industry observers note that you need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is python.

At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS.

In a recent development, no key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help.

On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type CLAWDOS. Later builds enhancement the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG).

In a recent development, /model, /chats, /memories, /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens a chat.

In a recent development, clawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its COPYING). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it.

ClawDOS stands on mTCP, FreeDOS, Open Watcom, the PicoMEM, 86Box and DOSBox-X.

Jolly, the mascot of Meta’s Muse AI agent.

Meta has put its Muse AI agent into a Chrome sidebar. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, announced the Muse Chrome extension in a post on X on Friday. He said 200,000 people were already using it.

Recent findings suggest that muse browses in the user’s own Chrome and acts only inside its own group of tabs, Digital Trends reported from the Chrome Web Store listing. Meta says Muse cannot see saved passwords, browsing history or Chrome settings. The listing also warns that Muse may take unexpected actions. Its activity may show up in a user’s Google account.

The Muse Charm is a keychain-sized device for talking to the agent. Meta plans to charge $300 for it, The Information’s Jyoti Mann reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The Charm will come with up to 12 months of free 5G data from Verizon, according to the report.

Meta has delayed its smartwatch to next year to focus on the Charm, The Information reported. Mark Zuckerberg showed the device at Meta Connect in September and mentioned it would ship in time for the holidays.

“We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon,” Meta’s Tyler Yee told The Information.

Some Instagram consumers are asking Muse to find and unfollow accounts that do not follow them back, WIRED’s Jason Parham reported on Friday. One user told WIRED he had heard of people losing their accounts for purging followers with third-party apps. He did not believe Muse could do it until he tried.

Recent findings suggest that muse went live in Australia on Tuesday, Meta confirmed. Owners can connect it to Gmail, Google Calendar, Instagram and OpenTable. Local partners such as Canva, Domain, Kogan, Officeworks and Ticketek will follow gradually.

“People stay in control, including choosing what Muse can access and approving purchases before they happen,” mentioned Meta’s Will Easton.

Industry observers note that muse has drawn 10 million consumers since its September launch. Meta states it runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated cloud computer. It keeps passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s view.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

Recent findings suggest that if you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the manufacturer is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

Industry observers note that the standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

It has been revealed that amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

It has been revealed that sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Health: Prime owners get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV demonstrates, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers upcoming free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

Monitoring new customers is the most vital part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:.

Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Tesla has started offering rides in its Cybercab in Dallas, the second city after Austin for the two-seater with no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla already runs Model Y robotaxis in Dallas and plans to start delivering Cybercabs to private buyers in Texas in December.

Tesla’s Cybercab, its two-seat robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals, is now giving rides in Dallas, InsideEVs reported. “Cybercab has arrived in your city,” Tesla’s Robotaxi account posted on X on Thursday.

Dallas is the second city to get the Cybercab, after it began giving rides in Austin in September. Tesla already runs driverless Model Y robotaxis in Dallas. Riders book both in the Tesla Robotaxi app.

In a recent development, tesla’s robotaxis also run in Houston, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Tampa, Orlando and Miami, mostly with the Model Y. It has focused on Texas and Florida, where the rules are looser than in states like California.

According to recent reports, the US road safety agency, NHTSA, is looking into how Tesla decided a car with no wheel or pedals meets US safety rules. Unlike Amazon’s Zoox, Tesla did not ask for an exemption. NHTSA is also reviewing claims that Tesla robotaxis, including Cybercabs, sped in school zones.

According to recent reports, tesla is also starting to sell the Cybercab to some customers for $29,990. Owners must pay a $299 monthly fee, or the car will not run. The first cars should reach buyers in Texas in December.

To build more of them, Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck output at its Texas plant around mid-2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

According to recent reports, in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also demonstrates how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

These 14 Newly introduced Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov.
  • In a recent development, technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this upgrade isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially rolls out the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 upcoming features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

In a recent development, technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this newly introduced feature here.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 also comes with a upcoming setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

Industry observers note that with watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

It has been revealed that the company generated some controversy when it first unveiled these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these newly introduced Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company indicates Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing newly introduced abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These latest actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Industry observers note that apple started testing its latest Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

In a recent development, continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training proposal. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Sources indicate that apple is also testing a upcoming Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Sources indicate that another upcoming Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing upcoming StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

Industry observers note that "Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with significant iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Sources indicate that apple is also rolling out upcoming languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

In a recent development, if you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the upcoming updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).

Geospace (GEOS -31.42%) reported significant revenue declines and widened net losses for fiscal year 2026, prompting a comprehensive operational restructuring to align costs with a challenging macroeconomic environment. Management stated that global energy disruptions, trade policy shifts, and government procurement delays pressured results across all three business segments. The organization entered fiscal year 2027 with a backlog exceeding $100 million and a revised sales strategy for its smart water products to drive a return to profitability.
