📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that new titles land on Netflix so often that the hardest part of movie night isn't making the popcorn; it’s deciding what to actually watch. It’s all too easy to get caught in the "what to watch" trap, especially when the streamer’s November 2026 slate hasn't let up, adding 51 movies at the start of the month and even more every single week.

With the weekend rolling around again, we here at Tom’s Guide want to save you the endless scrolling and have pulled together three fresh arrivals worth your time. Whether you’re a horror fan ready for the latest chilling installment of a long-running supernatural franchise, in the mood for a heartfelt road-trip dramedy starring Robert De Niro and Bobby Cannavale, or eager to start the Christmas countdown early (ugh, really?) with a holiday comedy that reunites the Lawrence brothers, we've got you covered.

That lineup should keep you busy over the next couple of days, and you might just come away with a upcoming favorite. Here are three new-to-Netflix movies to add to your weekend watchlist.

It has been revealed that bobby Cannavale has built a career on brash, combustible live wires, but “Ezra” makes for one of his most tender performances by far. He's a father who’ll risk everything for his autistic son in this movie, and knows how to tug on those heartstrings.

Directed by Tony Goldwyn (“Conviction,” “A Walk on the Moon”), this flick follows Max Bernal (Cannavale), a stand-up comic who’s torched his career and his marriage and moved back in with his father, Stan (Robert De Niro). Life is hardly going the way he planned, but somehow he's getting through it.

Sources indicate that when doctors want to medicate his young son Ezra (William A. Fitzgerald) and move him to a special school as a way to "treat" his autism, Max makes a reckless call and takes the boy on an unplanned cross-country road trip instead, hoping to bring about some changes in the pair's lives.

Recent findings suggest that watch "Ezra" on Netflix on Nov. 20.

The Lawrence brothers made their names on ’90s TV, from Joey’s “whoa”-laden performance on “Blossom” to Matthew’s appearance on “Boy Meets World,” and they've reunited for the holiday comedy “Marry Christmas.”.

Directed by Andrew Lawrence, the film casts Joey and Matthew Lawrence as the Wright brothers (no, not those), two newly engaged siblings who realize they’ve booked the same venue for competing weddings on Christmas Day. A rivalry breaks out over which brother gets to tie the knot on the holiday.

If you want a feel-good '90s-inspired comedy that gives all the Lawrence brothers a chance to feel like they're really doing something, this is it. And you'll have a good time bopping along with the two grooms while thinking about Christmas during simpler times.

Watch "Marry Christmas" on Netflix starting Nov. 21.

The "Insidious" franchise spent five films and more than a decade haunting the Lambert family, but its sixth chapter, “Insidious: Out of the Further,” hands the nightmares to someone entirely upcoming. That's good news if you haven't gotten caught up with the movies just yet.

Directed by Jacob Chase (“Come Play”), this entry stars Amelia Eve as Gemma, a mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, who discovers she can cross into the Further, the realm of lost souls at the heart of the series.

Once the demons work out what she can do, our world becomes their playground. Franchise mainstay Lin Shaye returns as parapsychologist Elise Rainier, but otherwise this is a pretty good entry point for anyone who wants to see what all the fuss is about.

Watch "Insidious: Out of the Further" on Netflix on Nov. 21.

  • Sources indicate that anthropic is a pure-play AI company founded in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees who thought that company was too weak on safety.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic's IPO also gave the company a chance to have the investing world's full attention, and CEO Dario Amodei spoke for about five minutes at the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday, sharing his vision for the company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:05PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

The torch in AI has been passed.

Sources indicate that it seems fitting in some ways that Anthropic's (ANT -8.50%) IPO came just a week after Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, leaving the chipmaker in turmoil. Nvidia had been the stock market's avatar for AI since the launch of ChatGPT, but with Anthropic now becoming the first AI lab to go public, it's set to take over as the market's best reflection of AI sentiment.

Sources indicate that anthropic is a pure-play AI company founded in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees who thought that company was too weak on safety. Anthropic builds AI models and software products based on its frontier intelligence platform, Claude.

It has been revealed that anthropic's IPO also gave the company a chance to have the investing world's full attention, and CEO Dario Amodei spoke for about five minutes at the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday, sharing his vision for the company. Here are three things investors should know about the newly public company, direct from Amodei.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

Anthropic has made its prioritization of safety clear from its inception, and AI safety has only become more salient amid concerns of AI models going rogue, escaping sandboxes, and the intensifying competition with China.

Anthropic's emphasis on safety may also be a competitive advantage at a time when AI is facing a backlash. The midterm elections reflected growing discontent with data centers and could lead to a slowdown or increased restrictions on them, at least in some states.

The emphasis on safety also acts in the company's interest in terms of liability and reputational damage, as the future of AI is wide open and will be determined by companies like Anthropic.

Amodei told the audience, "There's a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety, and an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start.".

Amodei wants everyone, including investors, customers, and AI skeptics, to know that he's one of the good guys.

In a similar vein, Amodei described a best-case scenario for the AI competition as a "race to the top.".

Amodei said, "If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful firm, others will be inspired to do the same.".

Sources indicate that if that spirit takes hold in the industry, then, he said, everybody wins, no matter who has the best models. Amodei assured investors that they intend to lead that race, saying, "The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.".

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Amodei began his comments with a story about how his father died of a disease, Hepatitis C, that was cured just a few years later.

The event clearly showed Amodei the power of invention and fresh technology, and after beginning his career in biology, he moved over to artificial intelligence, where he sees the potential for tremendous breakthroughs in medicine and beyond.

The departure of Jensen Huang due to a scandal involving multiple affairs is a reminder of the importance of character in leadership, and Amodei seems to possess that sufficiently.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic is a mission-driven company and the rare public benefit corporation on the stock market. Amodei brings a deep commitment to that mission and a personal passion for research and intelligence that can cure diseases and solve humanity's most pressing problems.

That's good news for Anthropic investors and should reassure them at a time when the AI trade looks more wobbly than ever.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We don't know about you, but with the chaos of the holidays coming up, the last thing we want is to waste precious brain cells trying to decide what to watch next. That's where Tom's Guide comes in: We do the work of regularly sifting through the best streaming services and their seemingly endless options of latest movies and television indicates, and compile an easy, breezy TV guide of what exactly you should be clicking "Play" on a given weekend.

And this weekend is no exception: We've sorted through what's recently arrived on Netflix, HBO Max, Paramount Plus, and more and narrowed things down to a trio of great watches, one for each night of your weekend.

In a recent development, on Friday evening, you can hang out with "The Altruists"; the Netflix true-crime drama centers on the biggest crypto fraud in history. Consider Saturday a pseudo date night with one of the world's most legendary chefs, with the HBO Max premiere of the Anthony Bourdain biopic, "Tony." And a lazy Sunday sounds like the perfect day to catch up with the ladies of "Yellowjackets," as the survival thriller kicks off its fourth and final season this week.

Recent findings suggest that that's a solid weekend of streaming sorted, no? All you have to do is grab some snacks and the remote.

If you love tech-world dramas like "The Dropout," "The Audacity" and "Super Pumped: The Battle for Uber," you'll likely enjoy "The Altruists," a true-crime saga centered on the whirlwind rise and catastrophic collapse of the multi-billion-dollar crypto exchange FTX, which premiered on Netflix on Thursday, November 19.

Starring Anthony Boyle as FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried and three-time Emmy winner Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison—the CEO of FTX's sister hedge fund Alameda Research and Sam's on-and-off-again girlfriend—the eight-part limited series follows the couple's transformation from ambitious young idealists trying to revolutionize the finance world to culprits in an $8 billion scheme that upended the entire crypto market.

The stacked ensemble cast includes Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Matt Rife, Madison Hu, Paul Reiser, Jennifer Grey, Robin Weigert and "Heated Rivalry" star Hudson Williams.

Stream "The Altruists" on Netflix now.

If you don't know him for his cooking, then you do for his cool: The late, great Anthony Bourdain was one of the most singular figures to come out of the culinary world, so it's no surprise that he'd be the subject of a high-profile bio-drama.

In a recent development, but instead of charting Bourdain's days as a hotshot chef in top New York kitchens, this Matt Johnson-directed biopic takes it back to the toque's beginnings as an impulsive 19-year-old (played by "The Holdovers" standout Dominic Sessa) working a summer dishwasher job at a local restaurant in 1970s Provincetown, Massachusetts. Under the tutelage of Chef José Vatel (Antonio Banderas) and the gritty restaurant crew, Tony B. gets his first real taste of the chaos and triumphs of a professional kitchen.

The A24 flick—which also stars Emilia Jones, Leo Woodall, Stavros Halkias, and real-life chef icon Eric Ripert—will make its subscription streaming debut on HBO Max on Saturday, November 20.

According to recent reports, the final chapter of "Yellowjackets" is finally here, with the survival drama's fourth season premiering on Paramount+ on Friday, November 20. But if you, like yours truly, are a bit behind on the psychological thriller, a long Sunday catching up with the unhinged antics of Shauna (played by Sophie Nélisse in the past and Melanie Lynskey in the present), Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown and Tawny Cypress), Misty (Samantha Hanratty and Christina Ricci) and the rest of the gang sounds like a day well spent.

Recent findings suggest that if you're not familiar, "Yellowjackets" follows a 1996 high school girls' soccer team in the aftermath of a plane crash, which leaves them stranded deep in the remote Canadian wilderness. Their fight for survival descends into a psychological nightmare as the girls begin dabbling in ritualized cannibalism, group hunts, and other cultish mysticism. In a parallel timeline set in the present day, the adult survivors must reckon with those dark secrets and long-held regrets 25 years later.

Stream "Yellowjackets" on Paramount+ now.

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” indicates Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Industry observers note that optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The firm’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

It has been revealed that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Upcoming Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon claims this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How substantial do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also vital to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

Sources indicate that the startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the manufacturer’s tech to beat GPUs.

Sources indicate that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr claims.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

Sources indicate that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the firm is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

It has been revealed that “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen states, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr notes. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another major advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

According to recent reports, “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” states Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

According to recent reports, one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Recent findings suggest that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Industry observers note that Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the tech giant announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

In a recent development, the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main glitch is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Recent findings suggest that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the tech giant believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch indicates.

In a recent development, the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

Sources indicate that lightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

It has been revealed that lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Sources indicate that lightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi claims. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

In a recent development, yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Upcoming, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

Sources indicate that the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Fresh, Optalysis.

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

It has been revealed that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Latest indicates that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

In a recent development, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Recent findings suggest that whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” claims Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia.

Recent findings suggest that take-Two states Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79B in sales worldwide through the end of its launch day, and sold 32.5 million units before release. The firm calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history, ahead of any film, album or game.

Grand Theft Auto VI made $3.79B in sales worldwide by the end of its launch day on Thursday, publisher Take-Two mentioned on Friday. It called the game the biggest entertainment launch in history, across any medium.

It has been revealed that the game also sold 32.5 million units before release, a record, according to Take-Two. The sales figure is a manufacturer estimate, and Take-Two did not say how it was calculated.

“It is with immense gratitude that we enter a fresh chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” mentioned Sam Houser, Rockstar’s founder and president.

For comparison, GTA V made $800M in its first 24 hours in 2013, and $1B in three days, Bloomberg reported. The biggest film opening, Avengers: Endgame, took about $1.2B worldwide over a weekend in 2019.

Take-Two had stated pre-orders beat expectations, and the game tied Metacritic’s record with a score of 99.

Analysts estimated it cost up to $1.5B to make, which Take-Two has not confirmed. Take-Two’s CEO has said Rockstar built it without generative AI.

It has been revealed that the game costs $80, or $100 for an edition with extra in-game items. A PC version and an online mode will follow later. Take-Two shares rose about 2.7% on Friday.

iOS 27.3 is at the moment in beta testing with developers and public beta people. The revision includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

It has been revealed that as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

According to recent reports, the redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

Recent findings suggest that the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 customers, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a latest Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week aims based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

Industry observers note that for iPhone Duo owners, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

It has been revealed that reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 also brings a fresh face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

According to recent reports, finally, iOS 27.3 includes a fresh option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

In a recent development, when it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with upcoming clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

It has been revealed that this includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The patch also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the revision expands Siri AI with many upcoming capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these fresh capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so consumers can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

According to recent reports, with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple claims it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to latest languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

According to recent reports, iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

Sources indicate that iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

In a recent development, for Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a upcoming “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The enhancement also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

There are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Recent findings suggest that second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a newly introduced “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

10 stocks we like better than Colgate-Palmolive ›.

Choosing between a steady staples giant and a premium apparel leader requires balancing reliability against growth potential. Investors must decide if Colgate-Palmolive (CL +1.89%) or lululemon athletica (LULU -2.76%) better suits their 2027 goals.

Colgate-Palmolive dominates everyday essentials like toothpaste and pet nutrition, while Lululemon leads the premium athletic wear market. One offers defensive qualities in volatile markets, and the other aims for expansion in international retail. This comparison looks at their growth paths, financial health, and current valuations to help you navigate these two distinct paths.

Recent findings suggest that colgate-Palmolive reaches consumers in more than 200 countries with a diverse portfolio including oral care, home hygiene, and specialty pet nutrition. In its latest annual report, Walmart (WMT +1.51%) and its affiliates accounted for nearly 11% of total net sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, though the organization continues to expand its presence in emerging markets among consumer staples stocks.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $21.3 billion, reflecting a growth rate of roughly 5.9%. Net income for the same period was close to $2.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of nearly 9.6%. These results indicate a consistent demand for hygiene and pet health products despite broader economic shifts.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached approximately 158.4x, which represents the relationship between its total debt and shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, was roughly 0.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $3.6 billion.

It has been revealed that lululemon Athletica operates a premium athletic lifestyle business focused on technical apparel, footwear, and accessories. The tech giant uses an omni-channel approach, selling through over 800 stores and its own digital platforms. The company also uses license and supply arrangements with third parties to enter international markets like the UAE and Israel.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached nearly $11.1 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 1.7%. Net income for this period was roughly $1.4 billion, resulting in a net margin of nearly 12.8%. The slower revenue growth suggests a period of normalization following years of rapid post-pandemic expansion.

Sources indicate that as of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.4x, showing the tech giant uses relatively little debt compared to its equity. The current ratio was approximately 2.3x, suggesting a strong ability to cover short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow reached close to $921.7 million.

Recent findings suggest that colgate-Palmolive faces significant exposure to international markets and fluctuations in foreign currency values. The firm deals with intense global competition from traditional rivals like Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG) and newer private-label manufacturers. It also manages substantial legal uncertainty regarding ongoing talc-related litigation and operational risks from potential supply chain disruptions.

Lululemon Athletica manages heightened competition in the athletic apparel market, especially from imitation products. The company is vulnerable to supply chain disruptions because its manufacturing and fabric sourcing are concentrated in the APAC region. Additionally, it faces reputational risks from pending securities class action lawsuits and sensitivity to changes in U.S. tariff policy.

Lululemon Athletica appears significantly cheaper than its peer, as it carries a lower Forward P/E and a lower P/S ratio, which measures sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Industry observers note that I'd go with Colgate-Palmolive. It sells everyday products around the world and has raised its dividend for 63 straight years, a record built on things people buy in any economy. It holds the biggest share of the world's toothpaste market, and its Hill's pet food brand adds a second source of growth.

Industry observers note that last quarter, sales grew in nearly every region, emerging markets like India and Brazil led the way, and management raised its profit outlook. Costs are rising and U.S. shoppers are cautious, but those pressures are hitting the whole industry, and the rest of Colgate's business is still growing.

Sources indicate that to be fair to lululemon, it has a premium brand and $1.4 billion in cash. But sales are shrinking, with North American shoppers buying less at existing stores, and the company cut its full-year outlook in its latest report. What's more, a new CEO is still reshaping the leadership team. For investors who want to buy and hold into 2027 and beyond, Colgate offers steady growth and a dividend that gets bigger every year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI dropped two new AI models this week in the form of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, each surpassing benchmarks of their predecessors, but people who have begun using them haven’t all walked away very happy.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced AI model seems to drop almost every couple of days from one of the significant tech giants, each improving on the previous version in one way or another. However, OpenAI’s latest and greatest are getting some pushback from developers and early testers. For the everyday user, the 6.2 Sol and Astra should perform more than serviceably, but those looking to dig in, test and use the new models for more professional work may run into some hiccups they’re not used to, according to some feedback.

Ethan Mollick, associate professor and director of the Generative AI Lab at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business, mentioned in a LinkedIn post that GPT-6.2 Astra was “harder to steer and work with,” and “frequently seemed ‘lazy’,” compared with competitor models. Another brutal assessment on LinkedIn came from Jason J. Fleagle, head of AI at NETSYNC: “I think GPT-6.2 has to be one of the worst AI models OpenAI has ever released.”.

However, there might be more to the story than that. OpenAI Codex leader Thibault Sottiaux, known as Tibo, mentioned in an X post that early builds of 6.2 Sol and Astra were released to influencers some time ago, that updates and changes were made to the models within the past couple of days, and that he assumes no retesting was done since. Only time and more testing will show whether these improvements make much of a meaningful difference.

OpenAI didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media owners.
  • In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.
  • According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta launched an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media owners. The firm, however, is not retreating.

In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.

According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta launched an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.

Meta’s goal of approaching young owners where they spend the most time offline was not a secret. As recently as late September, the company stated it was expanding its School Partnership Program, which includes 17,000 schools, with a stated goal to “help students and parents stay informed.”.

Sources indicate that the company’s internal documents reveal some of the motivations behind Meta’s push for school adoption and Project Gryffindor’s proposed features, such as school banners on teen profiles and the ability to search school directories by class year. The details were acquired as part of discovery in a multistate lawsuit over whether social media platforms are designed to be addictive to people under 18. Meta is a defendant in the case, along with other companies, including TikTok, Snap and Google.

According to recent reports, in 2024, Instagram introduced Teen accounts and has since been trying to assure parents they’re safe while rolling out additional protections. Studies, however, have suggested that young teens regularly encounter unsafe content or deal with unwanted contact. Recruiting more customers at an early age without resolving these risks could make teens more vulnerable to mental health problems and increase the chances of being bullied or harassed.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that to anyone familiar with Meta’s long history of privacy oversteps on platforms like Facebook, the documents aren’t surprising. They reveal a manufacturer primed to give school-age children latest ways to chat and connect with each other, and to encourage them to bring their friends along, expanding Instagram’s user base and engagement.

Industry observers note that like other social platforms, Instagram primarily makes its money from targeted advertising. User retention is a key part of Meta’s strategy.

In one of the document slides, titled “Why schools, why now?” which preceded Gryffindor’s launch, Meta noted, “Competitors are exploring school social use cases, but IG may be better positioned for school connections thanks to our differentiator of meeting upcoming people and building relationships with acquaintances.” In other words, Instagram’s size and scale, with about 3 billion active consumers globally, automatically make it a draw for students.

The NPR report comes within a week of a filing against Meta alleging that it’s withholding evidence in a major case involving social media’s effects on teenagers.

Recent findings suggest that one of Meta’s marketing pitches for its School Partnership Program is that it’s trying to create online safe spaces for students, while giving parents and schools more oversight on what’s accessible on the platform. But experts warn that Meta’s history makes it hard to trust the tech giant with protecting kids from predators or scammers.

Katie Paul, director of the Center for Accountability’s Tech Transparency Project, which has been researching how Meta handles child-safety concerns, noted that Instagram Teen accounts “are not safe as advertised” and that nothing is “legally requiring the tech giant to make these safe.” Paul pointed out that Instagram launched these accounts only when lawsuits over social media harm started rolling in.

Industry observers note that “It’s all part of a broader marketing (effort) to claim that these are just safer for kids because they are Teen accounts,” Paul mentioned. That marketing effort has included paid endorsements from therapists, psychologists and parent influencers to promote Teen accounts. The case for building up partnerships with schools is a way of “passing the buck on responsibility” to schools and parents, Paul said.

Parents, in particular, have less power in Instagram’s school groups: Unlike the school administrators tasked with managing school groups, parents have no powers to moderate or manage those groups; they can only view them. For Teen accounts in general, parents can’t view direct messages sent to or received by their children.

According to recent reports, meta’s business interests in its push for student engagement and school partnerships are easy to see through. Because kids are likely to be lifetime users on these platforms, getting them hooked early has long-term financial value.

“Ultimately, Meta is the one profiting off of the data collection of these kids while simultaneously failing to keep them safe,” Paul said.

The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go. The Segway E3 Go is made for those with more modest demands for their commute; priced at $649 — but often on sale for less — it also places a more modest demand on your wallet.

I rode the Segway E3 Go for a couple of weeks to get a feel for this mid-range commuter scooter, and to see how it compared to some of the best electric scooters I’ve tested over the years.

Sources indicate that the Segway E3 Go came out in 2026, and retails for $649, though you can often find it on sale for less than $500. For example, for Black Friday, it's discounted to $449 right now.

Segway has put a lot of thought into the feel of its scooters; in recent years, it’s started bending its handlebars slightly back, like on a bike, which gave me a bit more control while I was out and about.

The E3 Go’s deck is also fairly spacious; unless you have gigantic feet, you should have no trouble positioning yourself on the scooter.

I’m also a fan of the E3 Go’s folding mechanism; there’s a small tab at the base of the downtube, which you simply press with your foot to unlock the front half of the scooter and fold it down.

It has been revealed that however, you’ll still need a bit of strength to carry it around, as the E3 Go weighs a meaty 46 pounds. The E3 Pro, which has dual suspension and a longer range, is actually six pounds lighter.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While it lacks the full suspension of its more expensive siblings like the E3 Pro, the Go still has a front suspension. It made for a much smoother ride when going over potholes and other bumps when compared with scooters that lacked such amenities.

In a recent development, built into the handlebars of the E3 Go are turn signals, which you activate using a thumb switch on the left handlebar; I’ve loved this addition to all electric scooters I’ve tested. I just wish the E3 Go had rear turn signals, like the Segway Max G3 Plus, as it’s hard for cars behind you to see the handlebar signals. I also wish that the E3 Go’s headlight were slightly bigger, and that you could adjust its angle.

It has been revealed that like most of Segway’s scooters, the E3 Go has Apple FindMy, so you can track it if it goes missing. You should always use a lock, but it’s an extra bit of protection.

It has been revealed that the 400W motor in the E3 Go proved good, but not great, at climbing hills. On a moderate 5% grade, the scooter slowed to around 10 MPH, which is respectable given its price; however, on a steeper hill with a 6.9% grade — which gets as steep as 10.8% — the E3 Go barely made it to the top, where the similarly-priced Apollo Dash made it up without matter. To be fair, Segway says that the E3 Go is rated to a max grade of 9% (18º slope).

Sources indicate that segway advertises the E3 Go as having a max range of 25 miles; if you set the scooter to its highest performance setting, that estimate drops to just 11.2 miles. I took the E3 Go out for a 5.5-mile ride, and at its conclusion it had 32% battery life remaining, which would mean I would have made it to a little over 8 miles before the battery was completely drained. Of course, your mileage will literally vary based on your weight and the type of riding you do.

It has been revealed that the Segway E3 Go is a good, capable scooter for the price. It should be especially useful in flatter urban areas, and will suit commuters well, so long as you don’t have any major hills to climb. If you have steeper terrain, I would recommend the Apollo Dash; while its ergonomics aren’t as good, it has more power than the Segway, and costs about the same, with many other similar features.

If you can spring for the extra $50, the Segway E3 Pro has dual suspension and a longer range than the E3 Go, and is just as comfortable to ride. Either way, if you have to contend with a lot of potholes, the Segway and its suspension is worth a second look.

Soon You Can Ask Siri About What’s Showing on Your iPad

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (344 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hey Siri, what’s the name of this blue plant on my screen?
  • In a recent development, in its newly introduced iPadOS 27.3 release, Apple is adding several new features for iPads — Siri mode in the camera app, window resizing by tapping and more tools in the Freeform whiteboard app.
  • In a recent development, on an iPhone, you can ask Siri about what’s in your camera frame.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hey Siri, what’s the name of this blue plant on my screen? You couldn’t ask your iPad that question before, but you’ll be able to soon.

In a recent development, in its newly introduced iPadOS 27.3 release, Apple is adding several new features for iPads — Siri mode in the camera app, window resizing by tapping and more tools in the Freeform whiteboard app. The features are being tested in beta and will be released to the general public sometime in December. The new OS will be available on all iPads that support iPadOS 27.

The release notes for iPadOS 27.3 are listed here.

In a recent development, on an iPhone, you can ask Siri about what’s in your camera frame. Siri can identify the object and perform a web search on it. You can also take action items, such as pointing the camera at a restaurant bill and asking Siri to split it if you want to split it with people you’re with.

That same functionality will soon be available on iPads, with the iPadOS 27.3 release. Maybe you want to identify a plant out in nature, or an historic building during a walking tour, or figure out how to replicate a tasty dish you just ordered at a restaurant.

Another new feature in iPadOS 27.3 will make it easier to make windows bigger. Let’s say you’ve got a few windows open on your iPad, but there’s one you want to enlarge. You’ll be able to double-tap the top of the window to enlarge it, then double-tap again to revert it to its original size.

Prior to the iPadOS 27.3 release, you had to drag a corner of the window to make it bigger or smaller.

Freeform is an iPad app that serves as a digital whiteboard for sketching and writing out ideas and collaborating. You can add photos, videos, text, PDFs and other items to the whiteboard — using your mouse, finger or Apple Pencil — and sync it across other Apple devices such as iPhones and Macs.

#28154. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the organization’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

It has been revealed that I’m a significant fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, customers should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy customers at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”.

In a recent development, apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an enhancement, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

It has been revealed that make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

Industry observers note that it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

It has been revealed that will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

It has been revealed that once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

Recent findings suggest that I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech consumers may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

In a recent development, is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

#28153. Industry News: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4738 w)
